paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving scene requires representing both its three-dimensional structure and how that structure changes over time. 4DGT learns this task from real-world videos captured by a single camera, using frames whose camera poses are known. Its central representation is a collection of four-dimensional Gaussians that describe the scene across space and time.

This representation gives static scenery and moving objects a common treatment, including objects that exist for different portions of a sequence. A Transformer predicts these Gaussians from rolling windows of 64 consecutive posed frames. The authors also introduce a training strategy for controlling Gaussian density, allowing the model to handle longer inputs across space and time while producing consistent scene representations.

At inference, 4DGT predicts a reconstruction directly through the network. The abstract reports a reduction from hours to seconds compared with optimization-based reconstruction. Despite training entirely on monocular posed videos, it can substantially outperform earlier Gaussian-based networks on real-world videos and match optimization-based accuracy on cross-domain videos. These results support direct learned reconstruction as a practical route to processing long, changing scenes.
neurips-2025-4dgt-learning-a-4d-gaussian.tldr: 4DGT reconstructs changing scenes from posed monocular videos using direct predictions of space-time Gaussians, cutting reconstruction time from hours to seconds.

paragraphs: Dynamic pricing methods often treat prices as continuously adjustable, although actual sellers may choose from a discrete menu. This paper studies how explicitly using that menu can improve contextual pricing. Its central point is conditional: the benefit depends on how many available price points there are relative to the number of pricing decisions.

The proposed algorithm, BayesCoxCP, combines Bayesian learning with a semiparametric Cox proportional hazards model. Its theoretical analysis bounds regret, the accumulated cost of decisions relative to an optimal reference. The bounds adapt to a parameter gamma describing price-grid sparsity relative to the time horizon T, alongside a term involving the contextual dimension d.

For gamma below one third, the reported high-probability upper bound scales as T raised to (1 + gamma)/2 plus the square root of dT, with logarithmic factors suppressed. At or above that threshold, the first term becomes T raised to two thirds. Numerical experiments also show substantial improvements over an existing method, particularly for sparse price menus. Together, these findings identify when discrete pricing structure can provide a useful learning advantage.
neurips-2025-a-bayesian-approach-to-cont.tldr: BayesCoxCP uses discrete price information in Bayesian contextual pricing, with regret guarantees and empirical gains that are especially favorable for sparse price grids.

paragraphs: A smartphone’s wide and ultra-wide cameras can capture complementary evidence about the same scene. Camera shake may blur the wide-angle video while the lower-resolution ultra-wide view preserves sharper details. This paper builds a video deblurring system around that asymmetry, using the ultra-wide stream as a reference for restoring the wide-angle frames.

The proposed AsLeD-Net repeatedly aligns reference features across time and combines them with features from blurry frames. Its adaptive local matching module refines those blurry features using nearby reference features selected through nearest-neighbor matching. A difference compensation module addresses spatial inconsistency and misalignment, helping the network reconcile information captured through lenses with different views.

A further reference-guided motion compensation module aligns information temporally to improve consistency between restored frames. These components address complementary problems: finding useful sharp detail, aligning it spatially, and carrying it through the video. The authors report extensive experiments against potential solutions for asymmetric-lens deblurring that validate the approach. The contribution is a method designed specifically to exploit the unequal but complementary information already available from mobile dual-camera systems.
neurips-2025-asymmetric-dual-lens-video-.tldr: AsLeD-Net uses sharper ultra-wide video to restore blurry wide-angle footage while aligning detail across lenses and time.

paragraphs: Audio Flamingo 3 is a fully open audio-language model intended to understand and reason about speech, environmental sound, and music. Its unified audio encoder, AF-Whisper, learns representations across all three categories. This shared foundation supports a broader range of audio interactions within one model.

The system can perform reasoning before answering when requested, conduct conversations involving multiple audio inputs, and support voice-to-voice interaction. It also handles audio understanding and reasoning over recordings up to ten minutes long, including speech. To develop these capabilities, the authors curate AudioSkills-XL, LongAudio-XL, AF-Think, and AF-Chat and organize training into a five-stage curriculum.

Using only open-source audio training data, AF3 achieves reported state-of-the-art results on more than twenty audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, including long-audio evaluations. It surpasses both open-weight and closed-source models trained with much larger datasets in these comparisons. The findings connect a unified audio representation, targeted training data, and staged learning with strong performance across several audio capabilities, rather than treating each capability as a separate system.
neurips-2025-audio-flamingo-3-advancing-.tldr: Audio Flamingo 3 combines unified audio encoding and staged training to deliver open speech, sound, and music reasoning with strong benchmark results.

paragraphs: Length generalization means solving problems longer than those encountered during training. Earlier approaches often target individual symbolic tasks, and changes that help those tasks can harm a practical language model’s broader abilities. This paper investigates whether models can learn a more transferable capacity to follow rules over longer inputs.

The authors introduce Meta Rule-Following Fine-Tuning, or Meta-RFFT, alongside a dataset containing 86 tasks across code execution, number processing, and symbolic and logical reasoning. Training spans many tasks and examples. The intended benefit is that an unseen task can then acquire length generalization through minimal fine-tuning or a single prompted example, reducing dependence on extensive task-specific retraining.

In one reported result, a 32-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on addition involving one to five digits reaches 95% accuracy on thirty-digit addition. The compared reasoning models score 72% and 32%. Addition was absent from the model’s rule-following pretraining, although short addition examples were used in subsequent fine-tuning. This distinction makes the result evidence for transferring a learned generalization strategy across tasks, followed by extrapolation to substantially longer instances.
neurips-2025-beyond-single-task-robust-m.tldr: Meta-RFFT trains across many rule-based tasks so models can generalize to longer instances of unseen tasks after limited adaptation.

paragraphs: Language models can produce plans that are incorrect or fail as tasks grow larger. This paper gives them a different role within classical planning: writing heuristic functions that guide an automated search. The planner performs the actual search for a valid plan, while the generated heuristic helps decide which states to explore first.

For each planning domain, an LLM produces several candidate heuristics as Python code. The authors evaluate those candidates on training tasks using greedy best-first search and retain the best performer. This procedure uses the model’s domain-specific suggestions while preserving the planner’s correctness: returned plans are correct, without implying that every possible task will be solved.

The selected heuristics solve substantially more unseen, larger tasks than direct LLM planning and outperform leading domain-independent heuristics in the reported comparisons. They are also competitive with the strongest domain-dependent learning approach despite using a Python planner against optimized C++ implementations. In some domains, they expand fewer search states, indicating more informative guidance. The results show how generating search guidance can turn language-model knowledge into effective planning support.
neurips-2025-classical-planning-with-llm.tldr: LLM-generated Python heuristics guide classical planners toward correct solutions and solve more unseen tasks than direct LLM planning in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Repairing software involves several distinct jobs: locating the problem, proposing a change, and checking whether the change works. Co-PatcheR starts from the observation that these jobs demand different workflows and expertise, making the entire pipeline difficult for one small model. It instead coordinates specialized reasoning models across the patching process.

One model handles localization and patch generation. Localization narrows down suspicious lines in two steps, while generation combines proposing a patch with critique. The validation stage uses two additional models to produce issue-reproducing tests with and without assertions and assess patch correctness. A majority-vote procedure then selects among candidate patches.

The system resolves 46% of SWE-bench-Verified using three models with fourteen billion parameters each. The abstract contrasts this with specialized state-of-the-art methods reaching up to 41% using a seventy-billion-parameter model. Ablation studies examine the training recipes, training-data quantity, model size, and inference-time scaling choices. These findings support specialization and collaboration as a way to improve software repair while reducing the model sizes and training resources required relative to the reported specialized alternatives.
neurips-2025-co-patcher-collaborative-so.tldr: Co-PatcheR coordinates three specialized fourteen-billion-parameter models to locate, generate, and validate software fixes, resolving 46% of SWE-bench-Verified.

paragraphs: Some experiments can encourage people to receive a treatment but cannot directly determine whether they take it. This creates a gap between the assigned encouragement and actual treatment. The paper studies average treatment-effect estimation in this setting when a binary instrument supplies the encouragement and its assignment can adapt to the experiment’s history.

The authors derive a semiparametric efficiency bound, describing the achievable statistical precision within their framework. They show that a variance-aware assignment rule minimizes this bound by balancing outcome noise with variability in compliance. Their AMRIV method combines an online policy that learns this allocation with a sequential estimator based on influence functions.

The analysis establishes efficiency, multiply-robust consistency, asymptotic normality, and explicit convergence rates. It also provides asymptotic confidence sequences that support inference as observations accumulate, retaining their stated asymptotic qualification. Empirical studies show improved efficiency and robustness relative to existing baselines. The central contribution is to design encouragement assignment and treatment-effect estimation together, so adaptive experimentation accounts for both noisy outcomes and the uncertainty introduced by noncompliance.
neurips-2025-efficient-adaptive-experime.tldr: AMRIV jointly adapts treatment encouragement and effect estimation to improve statistical efficiency when participants may not comply.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether organizing a language model’s existing abilities into explicit reasoning operations can improve mathematical problem solving. Its inspiration comes from cognitive psychology and cognitive architectures, where reasoning is described as a coordinated sequence of modular operations. The authors translate that idea into an agent-style tool-calling framework.

The model receives a small collection of predefined cognitive tools, each representing a particular reasoning operation. Crucially, the language model itself executes these tools. The approach therefore changes how the model organizes and invokes reasoning operations, providing an alternative route to eliciting reasoning alongside methods based on chain-of-thought training and reinforcement learning.

Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the authors report substantial gains for both closed and open-weight models compared with their base versions. For GPT-4.1 on AIME2024, first-attempt success rises from 32% to 53%, exceeding o1-preview in the reported comparison. The result contributes evidence to the debate about how much reasoning post-training creates versus reveals. It demonstrates that structured invocation can improve performance, without settling whether all such abilities originate during pretraining.
neurips-2025-eliciting-reasoning-in-lang.tldr: Giving language models a small set of self-executed cognitive tools substantially improves mathematical reasoning in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A hitting time measures how many steps a random walk is expected to take to reach one graph node from another. It is useful for analyzing networks, ranking items, making recommendations, and studying disease spread. Computing it through methods that inspect the entire graph can become expensive, so this paper develops estimators that access only local information.

The first algorithm exploits a connection to two independent random walks started at the source and destination. Their meeting time provides a point at which hitting-time computations can be truncated. The authors analyze the resulting estimator using a product-graph construction and concentration bounds for Markov chains.

A second algorithm adapts spectral cutoff techniques to account for the fact that hitting times are directional: reaching one node from another need not take as long as the reverse journey. The paper supplies algorithmic upper bounds and tight asymptotic lower bounds, connects estimation to distribution testing, and evaluates the methods on real and synthetic data. Together, these contributions address both scalable computation and the theoretical difficulty of estimating directional random-walk distances.
neurips-2025-estimating-hitting-times-lo.tldr: The paper develops local algorithms for estimating directional random-walk hitting times without accessing an entire graph.

paragraphs: Synthetic images can look convincing while still containing subtle irregularities in how nearby pixels relate. This paper studies two sources of such artifacts: deviations in latent distributions and smoothing introduced during decoding. Their visible consequences can appear in local texture, edge structure, and transitions between colors.

The authors use local pixel dependencies grounded in Markov Random Fields to reconstruct images from neighboring pixel information. This reconstruction exposes disruptions in texture continuity and edge coherence that can help distinguish generated images. FerretNet builds on these signals with a lightweight neural network containing 1.1 million parameters, making local image structure central to its detection approach.

Although trained exclusively on a four-class ProGAN dataset, FerretNet achieves a reported average accuracy of 97.1% on an open-world benchmark spanning twenty-two generative models. The breadth of that evaluation matters because the detector encounters generators beyond its training source. The result supports the usefulness of local dependency artifacts for detection across the tested generators, while the small network size addresses the computational cost of deploying a detector.
neurips-2025-ferretnet-efficient-synthet.tldr: FerretNet detects synthetic images through disrupted local pixel relationships, achieving 97.1% average accuracy across twenty-two generators with 1.1 million parameters.

paragraphs: Image stitching depends on aligning overlapping views and combining them into a coherent image. Poor lighting, haze, and other difficult conditions can damage the visual evidence needed for alignment, while moving objects introduce additional inconsistencies. This paper develops ACDIS to address these problems within a single stitching framework.

Its bidirectional consistency learning procedure iteratively combines differentiable image restoration with homography estimation, which estimates a geometric alignment between views. The homography component uses a Gaussian-distribution encoding. By placing restoration and alignment inside the same iterative process, the method addresses degraded image appearance together with the geometric matching problem.

For the final composition, the authors add motion constraints to reduce interference from moving scene content. They also introduce a benchmark covering varied parallax and low-light, hazy, and underwater scenes, making adverse conditions an explicit part of evaluation. Experiments report visually pleasing stitched images and better results than state-of-the-art methods. The contribution links an adverse-condition stitching method with a dataset designed to test the environmental and motion challenges motivating it.
neurips-2025-image-stitching-in-adverse-.tldr: ACDIS combines iterative restoration, geometric alignment, and motion-aware composition to improve image stitching under adverse conditions.

paragraphs: Training batches determine which examples a neural network spends its limited learning effort on. Conventional approaches can keep the proportions of different classes fixed throughout training, even as the model’s strengths and weaknesses change. Learn2mix makes those proportions adaptive, with the aim of reaching useful performance more quickly under constrained training resources.

The strategy gives greater attention to classes with higher error rates and continually revises the mixture as training progresses. The key change is therefore in how available data are integrated into batches. A class that remains difficult can receive more training attention, connecting the sampling process to the model’s current performance rather than a fixed allocation.

Benchmark experiments report faster convergence than existing approaches and improved results across classification, regression, and reconstruction tasks, including settings with imbalanced classes and limited resources. The authors also provide theoretical analysis supporting their empirical findings. These results suggest that the composition of training data over time is an important efficiency choice: adapting the mixture can improve how effectively a network uses a restricted training budget.
neurips-2025-learn2mix-training-neural-n.tldr: Learn2mix adapts batch class proportions toward higher-error classes, improving convergence and results under limited training resources.

paragraphs: Object re-identification asks whether observations depict the same object. Many existing methods assume that the available sensing modalities match across observations, which restricts their usefulness when those inputs differ. MDReID addresses this mismatch by learning representations intended to support image-level retrieval across different combinations of modalities.

The approach distinguishes information shared across modalities from information specific to an individual modality. Its Modality Decoupling Module explicitly separates these two kinds of features. A second component, Modality-aware Metric Learning, uses relationships between their distributions to improve both the separation and the ability to distinguish object identities. This design supports comparisons when modalities align as well as when they do not.

Experiments cover RGBNT201, RGBNT100, and MSVR310. In that order, the abstract reports mean average precision improvements of 9.8%, 3.0%, and 11.5% for matched modalities, plus average gains of 3.4%, 11.8%, and 10.9% for mismatched modalities. The findings support explicitly modeling shared and modality-dependent information as a way to make retrieval more flexible while also improving performance in conventional matched-input settings.
neurips-2025-mdreid-modality-decoupled-l.tldr: MDReID separates shared and modality-specific features to improve object retrieval with both matched and mismatched sensing modalities.

paragraphs: Estimating ocean surface nutrients from sparse measurements requires accounting for how currents transport and diffuse them. Treating the problem as ordinary image inpainting can miss the ocean’s changing, multiscale dynamics. In particular, small errors in unresolved eddies can spread through time and distort the reconstructed nutrient fields.

NUTS separates the reconstruction into two scales. A homogenized solver captures stable large-scale transport using filtered flow, while a refinement module restores mesoscale detail based on the remaining eddy field. This separation allows the model to represent finer variability without making the entire reconstruction depend on an unstable treatment of small-scale flow. Homogenization theory supplies guarantees supporting the stated stability and robustness.

The authors report that NUTS beats all evaluated data-driven baselines in global reconstruction and achieves site-level accuracy comparable to numerical models. On real observations, it reduces normalized root mean squared error relative to the best baseline by 79.9% for phosphate and 19.3% for nitrate. Ablation studies support both modules. The findings connect the two-scale physical design with improved reconstruction and resistance to mesoscale perturbations.
neurips-2025-nuts-eddy-robust-reconstruc.tldr: NUTS separates large-scale transport from eddy-driven detail to reconstruct ocean nutrients more accurately and robustly from sparse observations.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to help a larger target model generate text faster. A practical obstacle is that drafters are often trained for a particular target family, making reuse difficult when the target changes. OmniDraft addresses that compatibility problem while also adapting the drafter to user data during deployment.

The framework combines an online n-gram cache with hybrid distillation fine-tuning to handle vocabulary differences between draft and target models. It further uses adaptive drafting techniques to improve decoding speed. These mechanisms support the paper’s goal of reusing one drafter across targets and improving its behavior with continued use, especially in on-device applications.

The authors demonstrate online learning on mathematical reasoning, coding, and text-generation tasks. A single Llama-68M draft model pairs with Vicuna-7B, Qwen2-7B, and Llama3-8B, with reported speedups reaching 1.5–2 times. These examples substantiate compatibility across several model families and the potential for deployment-time adaptation. The speedup is a reported upper-range result, rather than a promise that every target, workload, or stage of use will benefit equally.
neurips-2025-omnidraft-a-cross-vocabular.tldr: OmniDraft lets one small draft model adapt online across target models with different vocabularies, reporting speedups of up to 1.5–2 times.

paragraphs: Streaming measurements often form multidimensional arrays, or tensors, with missing entries that need to be estimated as new data arrive. Traffic and weather are examples where the data continually expand across space and time. This paper proposes Online Functional Tensor Decomposition to represent that expanding information as a continuous function.

The method combines CP tensor decomposition with coordinate-based implicit neural representations. These networks parameterize the decomposition using coordinates, so newly arriving observations can be incorporated through new coordinate inputs. Updating the representation becomes a continual-learning problem: adjust the network to fit recent data while retaining knowledge of earlier observations.

To address forgetting, the authors introduce a long-tail memory replay method adapted to the local continuity of the neural representation. Replaying stored information supports retention as the model changes. Experiments on traffic, weather, user-item, and video data verify the approach’s effectiveness for streaming tensor completion. The contribution is a connection between classical tensor structure and continually updated neural functions, giving the model a way to accommodate an expanding stream without treating each update as an isolated reconstruction problem.
neurips-2025-online-functional-tensor-de.tldr: OFTD combines tensor decomposition, coordinate-based neural representations, and memory replay to complete streaming data while retaining earlier knowledge.

paragraphs: Generating indoor layouts requires placing objects coherently while meeting human design preferences. This paper addresses both the training-data problem and the model-training problem. It introduces 3D-SynthPlace, a dataset of nearly seventeen thousand scenes built by extending 3D-Front through GPT-generated layouts and human inspection.

The dataset covers bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens, and bathrooms, with varied objects and high-level spatial annotations. OptiScene, an open-source language model for layout generation, learns from this data in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning first teaches it to describe spatial relationships and then predict concrete placements conditioned on those descriptions. Multi-turn direct preference optimization subsequently aligns the layouts more closely with human preferences.

The authors report that preference optimization improves layout quality and generation success rates, and that OptiScene outperforms traditional prompt-driven and learning-based baselines in extensive experiments. They also report promising potential for scene editing and robot navigation. Those interactive uses extend the motivation beyond producing a static room arrangement, while remaining potential applications rather than a claim of fully established performance across all such tasks.
neurips-2025-optiscene-llm-driven-indoor.tldr: OptiScene uses human-inspected synthetic layouts and two-stage preference-oriented training to improve indoor scene generation.

paragraphs: Comparing language-model architectures at academic training scales can be difficult because randomness obscures differences in specific abilities. This paper introduces controlled synthetic pretraining tasks that isolate capabilities such as reasoning and knowledge manipulation. The aim is to make architectural effects easier to identify and study economically.

Within that framework, the authors identify Canon layers: lightweight components that form weighted sums of neighboring token representations. These layers encourage information exchange across nearby tokens and can be incorporated into Transformers, linear-attention models, and state-space models. Reported benefits include increased reasoning depth, with a twofold improvement given as an example, along with gains in reasoning breadth and knowledge manipulation.

The authors also report that Canon layers bring NoPE models up to RoPE performance and make linear attention competitive with strong linear models such as Mamba2 and GDN. They validate findings through synthetic tasks and real-world academic-scale pretraining. The broader proposal is that controlled tasks can expose abilities otherwise hidden by noisy comparisons. Their possible use in predicting future architectures under improved training pipelines remains a prospective claim.
neurips-2025-physics-of-language-models-.tldr: Controlled synthetic tasks reveal that lightweight Canon layers improve several language-model capabilities by mixing information across neighboring tokens.

paragraphs: A depth model can recover scene structure without knowing its absolute physical scale. This paper turns Marigold, a pretrained diffusion model for scale-invariant monocular depth, into a metric depth predictor by adding information from defocus blur. The conversion happens during inference and requires no additional model training.

The method captures two images from the same viewpoint, one with a small aperture and one with a large aperture. Their defocus information supplies a physical cue for recovering depth scale. Using a defocus-blur image formation model, the authors define a loss whose gradients update both the metric scaling parameters and Marigold’s noise latents during inference.

This design combines a pretrained model’s depth representation with evidence from a particular image pair. The paired aperture captures are a concrete input requirement, and training-free operation still involves inference-time optimization. On a self-collected real dataset, the authors report quantitative and qualitative improvements over state-of-the-art zero-shot metric depth methods. The findings support using physically grounded blur cues to adapt an existing scale-invariant predictor to absolute-depth estimation.
neurips-2025-repurposing-marigold-for-ze.tldr: The method recovers metric depth without retraining Marigold by optimizing against defocus cues from two same-viewpoint images captured at different apertures.

paragraphs: Improving fairness and safety in text-to-image generation can come at the expense of matching the prompt or preserving image quality. RespoDiff addresses this tension by changing intermediate bottleneck representations inside a diffusion model. Its design gives responsibility-related concepts and semantic preservation separate learnable components.

One module captures and enforces concepts such as fairness and safety. The other maintains semantic alignment with neutral prompts. A new score-matching objective coordinates their learning, so the two modules can pursue their respective goals together. This separation makes preserving the requested meaning an explicit part of the intervention, alongside the desired changes in generated content.

The authors report better responsible-generation performance than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining semantic alignment and image fidelity. They describe an improvement of approximately 20% in responsible and semantically coherent generation across diverse unseen prompts, without identifying a more specific metric in the abstract. The framework also integrates into SDXL. These findings support the dual-module design as a way to improve the evaluated responsibility objectives while retaining the visual and semantic qualities users expect.
neurips-2025-respodiff-dual-module-bottl.tldr: RespoDiff coordinates two bottleneck modules to improve fairness and safety in image generation while preserving prompt alignment and image quality.

paragraphs: A trading agent trained on historical data typically cannot change the recorded prices through its actions. In deployment, its own transactions can move market prices, creating a mismatch between training and actual trading. This paper studies robust reinforcement learning designed to account more faithfully for that market impact.

Robust methods evaluate policies against unfavorable possibilities within an uncertainty set. The authors argue that commonly used symmetric structures miss the directional nature of trading-induced price changes. They introduce a new class of elliptic uncertainty sets and derive both implicit and explicit closed-form characterizations of the worst-case uncertainty. These results make robust policy evaluation computationally tractable within their formulation.

Experiments cover both single-asset and multi-asset trading tasks. The method achieves a superior reported Sharpe ratio and remains robust as trade volumes increase. The results connect the geometry of the uncertainty model with trading performance under stronger market impact. The contribution is therefore both a more suitable uncertainty representation for this deployment mismatch and an efficient way to evaluate policies against the unfavorable cases it describes.
neurips-2025-robust-reinforcement-learni.tldr: The paper introduces tractable elliptic uncertainty sets for robust trading agents that account for directional market impact.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation creates a small synthetic training set intended to retain the usefulness of a much larger dataset. This paper examines backdoor attacks against condensation based on distribution matching. Such attacks aim to make a trained model behave maliciously on triggered inputs while preserving its performance on ordinary inputs.

SNEAKDOOR focuses on stealth in both the condensed training images and the triggered inference samples. Its design exploits vulnerabilities around class decision boundaries and uses a generative module to produce input-dependent triggers aligned with local feature geometry. The purpose of this coordination is to reduce conspicuous changes while retaining the influence needed to induce the backdoor behavior.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report a favorable balance between attack success, clean test accuracy, and stealth. They describe reduced visibility of synthetic-data artifacts and triggered-sample perturbations, including concealment from human inspection and statistical detection in the studied setting. The security significance is that preserving ordinary accuracy alone does not capture the problem: a condensed dataset can retain useful training behavior while also carrying a difficult-to-notice mechanism for manipulating later predictions.
neurips-2025-sneakdoor-stealthy-backdoor.tldr: SNEAKDOOR demonstrates stealthier backdoors in condensed datasets while maintaining strong attack success and ordinary test accuracy.

paragraphs: Evaluating a model separately across population subgroups is important for examining fairness, but equal scores do not automatically imply fair behavior. This paper shows why interpreting those scores requires understanding how the data were generated. Even representative data can reflect existing social disparities that make performance equality an unreliable fairness criterion.

Selection bias creates a further challenge when the observed data do not represent the relevant population. In that situation, both subgroup evaluation and alternatives based on conditional independence testing may be invalid unless the analysis makes explicit assumptions about the selection process. Changing the statistical test alone does not resolve uncertainty about how people or observations entered the dataset.

The authors use causal graphical models to characterize fairness properties and the stability of subgroup metrics under different data-generating processes. Their framework suggests combining disaggregated evaluation with explicit causal reasoning about confounding and distribution shift, potentially using conditional independence tests and weighted performance estimates. The practical implication is to treat subgroup metrics as evidence requiring interpretation within a causal account of the data, rather than as a self-sufficient verdict on fairness.
neurips-2025-understanding-challenges-to.tldr: Subgroup performance comparisons can mislead fairness assessments unless their interpretation accounts for real-world disparities, selection bias, and causal assumptions.

paragraphs: Trajectory models often specialize in a particular task or region and can be sensitive to how movement data are collected. UniTraj aims to build a more broadly reusable foundation for modeling trajectories. The work addresses this through a geographically diverse dataset, pretraining strategies for heterogeneous traces, and a flexible model architecture.

The authors construct WorldTrace with 2.45 million trajectories containing billions of GPS points across seventy countries. Adaptive Trajectory Resampling and Self-supervised Trajectory Masking support learning from traces with different sampling rates and quality. The architecture is designed to capture complex movement patterns while accommodating multiple trajectory tasks, connecting diversity in the training data with flexibility in downstream use.

Experiments across several tasks and real-world datasets report consistent improvements over existing methods, including stronger scalability, adaptability, and generalization. WorldTrace is presented as a particularly suitable training resource, but the model is not restricted to that dataset. The findings support the combined approach to reducing task and regional dependence; the aspiration toward universal modeling is grounded in those evaluated tasks and datasets rather than a claim of demonstrated coverage of every movement setting.
neurips-2025-unitraj-learning-a-universa.tldr: UniTraj combines worldwide GPS data, adaptable pretraining, and a flexible architecture to improve trajectory modeling across tasks and regions.
